declared.title: A Cross-Cultural and Intra-Cultural Investigation of the Misinformation Effect in Eyewitness Memory Reports
declared.foundIn: OpenAlex search « cross-cultural differences susceptibility misinformation effect false memory culture » (2026-11-23)

population: 127 adults in Ghana (n = 65) and the UK (n = 62), taken as a collectivistic and an individualistic culture by Hofstede's country index

findings.text: On a recognition test, people from the collectivistic culture (Ghana) accepted more misleading details than people from the individualistic culture (UK)

support.sentence: However, participants from the collectivistic culture endorsed more misleading items in the recognition task than those from the individualistic culture.

findings.text: In free recall, the two cultures did not differ in how many misleading details they reported

support.sentence: Cultural differences in misinformation endorsement were not observed in free recall.

findings.text: In recognition, people picked the misleading version of central details more often than for control details: the misinformation was manipulated within each person

support.sentence: There was also a significant main effect of misinformation on the endorsement of misleading items about central details F(1,25) = 41.87, p < .001, ηp2 = .25.
support.readBy: memory-rewritten reviser, 2026-11-26: submitted version (Birmingham City University repository), Results, recognition

findings.text: In free recall, in their own words, only 18% of people reported at least one misleading detail (Ghana 20%, UK 16%)

support.sentence: Overall, 18% of the sample reported at least one item of misinformation in the free recall (Ghana = 20%; UK = 16%).
support.readBy: memory-rewritten reviser, 2026-11-26: submitted version (Birmingham City University repository), Discussion

limits: two small samples (127 people), one country per culture: the authors call their findings preliminary
culture was not assigned, and the self-construal scale found no difference between the groups (d = .21 and .01): « collectivistic » rests on the country index
the culture × misinformation interaction was significant for background details, not for central ones (p = .074)
only the misinformation effect is experimental; the culture findings compare groups (association)
Ghana and the UK, no Arab sample; Arab societies are often described as collectivistic, but that was not tested
